claims.text: The initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneously mixed and crystalline, with no significant elemental segregation.
Incremental heating in an inert atmosphere enhances surface diffusion in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface diffusion causes Cu to segregate preferentially to nanoparticle surfaces.
Cu enrichment at the nanoparticle surface lowers the local melting temperature.
The locally reduced melting temperature initiates a premelted state at the nanoparticle surface.
The surface premelted state propagates inward and triggers overall melting.
A Cu-enriched surface layer forms during heating.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituent elements.
Cu has a lower surface energy than the other constituent elements.
Heated nanoparticles should develop a liquid-like, disordered surface layer before complete melting.
Heated nanoparticles should show measurable Cu enrichment at their periphery.
Melting should initiate at the surface and progress inward as temperature increases.
Nanoparticles maintained below the premelting regime should retain uniform elemental distributions.
Nanoparticles maintained below the premelting regime should retain crystalline order.
Particle size, heating rate, and oxidative exposure may alter diffusion and segregation dynamics and thereby affect melting behavior.
Absence of detectable surface Cu enrichment before melting would falsify Cu-induced surface premelting as the governing mechanism.
Identical melting behavior in as-synthesized and homogenized nanoparticles, without a surface-initiated premelting front, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
